newsitem.title: JORDAN: Amman Bank for Investment forced to close.
newsitem.headline: Amman Bank for Investment forced to close.

text.p: A Jordanian court has ruled that the troubled Amman Bank for Investment, under Central Bank control since March, should be shut down because of heavy losses, a court official said on Saturday.
The court decision puts a legal seal on a deal with the Central Bank to liquidate Amman Bank for Investment and sell off its banking licence to Jordan's biggest bank, Arab Bank.

Jordan's Central Bank was quoted by the state news agency Petra as saying liquidation of Amman Bank came after the troubled bank failed to take advantage of chances afforded by the monetary authorities to restore its finances.
The bank was unable to raise its capital to 20 million dinars ($28 million) by bringing in new investors despite Central Bank incentives.
The bank's last annual meeting, in 1996, decided to restructure its capital by reducing it to five million dinars from 15 million dinars to wipe off some of its accumulated losses.

"The Central Bank tried to rectify the situation of Amman Bank through a number of plans but the bank was unable to follow them, which only worsened the problem and deepened its liquidity problem," an unnamed Central Bank source was quoted as saying.
Arab Bank will use the licence to set up Jordan's second Islamic bank. It says the Central Bank has agreed to underwrite all Amman Bank for Investment's losses and bad debts.
Aside from Arab Bank "no other local banks presented acceptable offers which met with the Central Bank's requirements", the source said.
The court official said that judge Mohammad Tarawneh ruled on Thursday that the bank be liquidated under Jordanian company law which forces liquidation if losses exceed 75 percent of paid up capital.
But the ruling may still be appealed by shareholders, the official said. They appear to have been the losers in the deal, bankers said.
The Central Bank took control of troubled Amman Bank for Investment last March, effectively putting the loss-making bank, one of Jordan's six investment banks, under its custody.
Amman Bank for Investment's accumulated losses stood at 33.8 million dinars ($48 million) at the end of November 1995, effectively eliminating the entire shareholders' equity, the Central Bank said.
